label: Causation from Correlation
oneLiner: Two things occur together, so one must cause the other.
definition: The argument infers a causal relationship from a correlation, overlooking reverse causation, a common cause, or coincidence.
objectives: Recognize causation from correlation in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “Every time I carry an umbrella, it rains—so carrying it brings rain.”
“Countries with independent central banks have lower inflation, so independence lowers inflation.” (reverse causation possible)
“Funds that hire star managers outperform, so stars cause outperformance.” (successful funds can afford stars)

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: two events linked by co-occurrence or sequence, and a causal conclusion
Match to answer language: “overlooks the possibility that … the reverse / some third factor / coincidence”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “overlooks the possibility that … the reverse / some third factor / coincidence”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Accepting a causal conclusion because the correlation is strong.

card.front: [Diagram: A ↔ B with a broken causal arrow] Name this flaw and its three alternatives.
card.back: Causation from correlation; alternatives: reverse causation, common cause, coincidence.

label: Unrepresentative Sample
oneLiner: A conclusion about a population rests on a sample unlike that population.
definition: The argument generalizes from a sample that is too small, self-selected, or biased toward a particular result.
objectives: Recognize unrepresentative sample in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “My three friends loved the film, so everyone will.”
“82% of an arbitration journal’s readers prefer arbitration, so most businesses do.”
“Surviving merchant letters mostly discuss Ottoman trade, so it dominated merchants’ concerns.” (survival bias)

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: a survey, study, or record set standing in for a larger group
Match to answer language: “draws a conclusion about a group from a sample that is unlikely to be representative”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “draws a conclusion about a group from a sample that is unlikely to be representative”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Focusing on sample size alone; bias matters more than size.

card.front: [Icon: magnifier over a tiny crowd] Name this flaw.
card.back: Unrepresentative sample: the sample differs from the population the conclusion concerns.

label: Part-to-Whole / Whole-to-Part
oneLiner: A property of the parts is assumed to belong to the whole—or vice versa.
definition: Composition assumes the whole has the properties of its parts; division assumes each part has the properties of the whole. Many properties do not transfer.
objectives: Recognize part-to-whole / whole-to-part in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “Every ingredient is delicious, so the dish will be delicious.”
“Every clause of the agreement is easy to understand, so the agreement is easy to understand.”
“The conglomerate is highly profitable, so each of its divisions is profitable.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: a property attributed to a group because its members have it (or the reverse)
Match to answer language: “presumes that what is true of each part is true of the whole” (or the reverse)
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “presumes that what is true of each part is true of the whole” (or the reverse)
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Missing the direction: part→whole (composition) vs. whole→part (division).

card.back: Composition (part-to-whole): conciseness of parts need not transfer to the whole.

label: Equivocation
oneLiner: A key word shifts meaning between premise and conclusion.
definition: The argument uses a term in two senses, so the premises connect to the conclusion only verbally.
objectives: Recognize equivocation in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “A feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; so a feather cannot be dark.”
“Inflation is ‘in effect a tax’; only the legislature may tax; so the central bank’s program is unconstitutional.”
“The company has a ‘strong balance sheet’ (lots of assets), so it is ‘strong’ (low risk).”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: the same word or phrase appears in premise and conclusion with different meanings
Match to answer language: “uses a key term in one sense in a premise and in a different sense in the conclusion”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “uses a key term in one sense in a premise and in a different sense in the conclusion”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Not noticing hedges like “in effect” or “in a sense” that signal a shift.

keyPoints.point: Premise and conclusion use it differently

card.front: [Diagram: a word splitting into two meanings] Name this flaw.
card.back: Equivocation: a key term changes meaning mid-argument.

label: Ad Hominem
oneLiner: Attacks the arguer instead of the argument.
definition: The argument rejects a claim because of the character, interests, or circumstances of the person making it, not because of the claim’s merits.
objectives: Recognize ad hominem in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “Don’t trust his diet advice—he’s overweight.”
“Reject the ambassador’s quota proposal: her country has a small fleet and loses little.”
“The analyst’s downgrade is meaningless; she was fired from her last bank.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: the speaker’s motives, character, or hypocrisy offered as a reason to reject a claim
Match to answer language: “attacks the person making the argument rather than the argument itself”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “attacks the person making the argument rather than the argument itself”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Confusing legitimate challenges to an expert’s reliability with attacks on the merits.

card.front: “Her proposal benefits her own country, so it should be rejected.” Flaw?
card.back: Ad hominem (circumstantial): attacks motives rather than the proposal’s merits.

label: Appeal to Authority
oneLiner: Relies on an authority outside its expertise—or as if authority were proof.
definition: The argument treats an authority’s endorsement as decisive when the authority lacks relevant expertise, or when authority alone cannot settle the question.
objectives: Recognize appeal to authority in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “A famous actor says this vitamin works, so it does.”
“A Nobel physicist says the treaty is unconstitutional, so it is.”
“A celebrated CEO predicts the currency will collapse, so hedge everything.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: a cited expert or celebrity carrying the whole argument
Match to answer language: “relies on the testimony of an authority whose expertise lies outside the matter in question”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “relies on the testimony of an authority whose expertise lies outside the matter in question”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Treating every citation of an expert as a flaw; relevant expertise is legitimate support.

card.front: “A renowned surgeon says the tax plan is unwise.” Flaw if offered as decisive?
card.back: Appeal to (inappropriate) authority—expertise outside the field.

label: Circular Reasoning
oneLiner: The conclusion is assumed in the premises.
definition: The argument’s premises presuppose the very claim to be proved, so it offers no independent support.
objectives: Recognize circular reasoning in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “This book is reliable because it says so in the book.”
“The statute is valid because valid statutes are those the legislature enacts—and this one is valid.”
“Our forecasts are accurate because our accurate forecasting model produced them.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: the conclusion (or a synonym) reappears as a premise
Match to answer language: “presupposes the truth of what it sets out to prove”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “presupposes the truth of what it sets out to prove”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Missing circularity when the conclusion is reworded.

card.front: [Icon: a circle of arrows] Name this flaw.
card.back: Circular reasoning: the premises assume the conclusion.

label: False Dichotomy
oneLiner: Presents two options as the only ones.
definition: The argument assumes only two alternatives exist and, rejecting one, embraces the other, ignoring further possibilities.
objectives: Recognize false dichotomy in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “Either we leave now or we miss the film.” (Later showings exist.)
“Either the court overrules the precedent or it endorses injustice.”
“Either we raise taxes or we default.” (Spending cuts, refinancing…)

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: “either… or…” framing with one option eliminated
Match to answer language: “assumes without warrant that only two options are available”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “assumes without warrant that only two options are available”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Accepting the framing because both options are plausible.

card.front: [Icon: a fork with a hidden third path] Name this flaw.
card.back: False dichotomy: assumes only two options exist.

label: Sufficient / Necessary Confusion
oneLiner: Treats a requirement as a guarantee—or a guarantee as a requirement.
definition: Reversal: from A → B and B, concludes A. Negation: from A → B and ¬A, concludes ¬B. Both confuse sufficient and necessary conditions.
objectives: Recognize sufficient / necessary confusion in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “You need a ticket to board; I have a ticket; so I’ll board.” (Requirement treated as guarantee.)
“Only audited firms list on the premium tier; Zentara was rejected; so it wasn’t audited.”
“Any treaty ratified is binding; the Accord is binding; so it was ratified.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: a conditional rule followed by an inference that runs backward or negates the wrong side
Match to answer language: “takes a condition that is necessary for X to be sufficient for X” (or the reverse)
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “takes a condition that is necessary for X to be sufficient for X” (or the reverse)
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Not distinguishing the reversal (B so A) from the negation (¬A so ¬B).

keyPoints.point: Negation: not A, so not B
Contrapositive is the only valid flip

card.front: [Diagram: A → B, with a red arrow drawn B → A] Name this flaw.
card.back: Sufficient/necessary confusion (reversal): affirming the necessary condition does not establish the sufficient one.

label: Absence of Evidence
oneLiner: No proof of X is treated as proof of not-X.
definition: The argument concludes a claim is false because it has not been proven true (or true because not proven false).
objectives: Recognize absence of evidence in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “No one has proven ghosts don’t exist, so they do.”
“Short-term studies found no harm, so the additive poses no long-term risk.”
“Auditors found no fraud in a sample of files, so there is no fraud.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: “has not been shown / no evidence” followed by a confident opposite conclusion
Match to answer language: “treats a lack of evidence for a claim as evidence that the claim is false”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “treats a lack of evidence for a claim as evidence that the claim is false”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Ignoring whether the investigation could even have detected the thing in question.

keyPoints.point: Could the search have found it?

card.front: [Icon: an empty evidence box] Name this flaw.
card.back: Absence of evidence: lack of proof treated as proof of the opposite.

label: Percentage vs. Number
oneLiner: Confuses rates or shares with absolute amounts.
definition: The argument moves from a percentage (share, rate) to a conclusion about numbers (amounts), or vice versa, ignoring changes in the base.
objectives: Recognize percentage vs. number in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “A larger share of my budget goes to rent, so I pay more rent.” (Budget may have shrunk.)
“Convictions rose as a share of cases, so more people were convicted.”
“Advertising’s share of revenue rose, so advertising revenue rose.” (Total may have fallen.)

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: percentages or shares in premises, counts or amounts in the conclusion
Match to answer language: “confuses a proportion with an absolute number”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “confuses a proportion with an absolute number”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Forgetting that the denominator can change.

card.front: [Icon: % sign] A rate rose; did the count rise?
card.back: Not necessarily—percentage vs. number: the base may have shrunk.

label: Possibility vs. Certainty
oneLiner: What might happen is treated as what will happen.
definition: The argument converts a possibility (“may”, “could”) into a certainty (“will”, “must”), or treats something unlikely as impossible.
objectives: Recognize possibility vs. certainty in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “It might rain, so the picnic will be cancelled.”
“Regulators may block the merger; if blocked, shares fall; so shares will fall.”
“A recession could hit, so the fund will lose money.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: modal words (may, could, possible) in premises; certain words (will, must) in the conclusion
Match to answer language: “treats as certain something that has only been shown to be possible”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “treats as certain something that has only been shown to be possible”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Not tracking modal words from premises to conclusion.

card.back: Possibility vs. certainty: what may happen is treated as what will happen.

label: Straw Man
oneLiner: Misrepresents a position, then refutes the misrepresentation.
definition: The argument distorts an opponent’s view—usually into a more extreme or foolish version—and attacks that instead of the actual view.
objectives: Recognize straw man in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “You want a later curfew? So you think teenagers should have no rules?”
“The senator wants higher capital reserves—evidently she wants to ban lending.”
“The CFO proposed trimming travel costs; apparently she wants to end all client meetings.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: “so you’re saying…” / “evidently X believes…” followed by an extreme paraphrase
Match to answer language: “distorts an opposing position and then argues against the distorted version”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “distorts an opposing position and then argues against the distorted version”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Missing it when the distortion is subtle (exaggerating scope or strength).

card.back: Straw man: refutes a distorted version of the opponent’s position.

label: Overgeneralization
oneLiner: Draws a broad conclusion from too few or atypical cases.
definition: The argument extends a conclusion from limited instances to a whole class without adequate basis.
objectives: Recognize overgeneralization in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “I got a bad meal there once—the restaurant is terrible.”
“One arbitration award was annulled, so arbitration is unreliable.”
“Two emerging-market funds failed, so emerging markets are uninvestable.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: one or a few cases → a universal or broad claim
Match to answer language: “draws a general conclusion from too few instances”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “draws a general conclusion from too few instances”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Confusing it with sampling bias (bias vs. sheer insufficiency).

card.front: [Icon: one point fanning to a wide arc] Name this flaw.
card.back: Overgeneralization: a broad conclusion from too few cases.

label: Comparison of Unlike Things
oneLiner: Draws a conclusion from an analogy between relevantly different cases.
definition: The argument assumes two situations are alike in a way that matters, when a relevant difference undermines the comparison.
objectives: Recognize comparison of unlike things in an unfamiliar argument
Match it to the abstract language LSAT answers use
Explain the flaw in your own words

examples.text: “Dogs love walks, so my cat will too.”
“The tribunal’s procedure worked in commercial cases, so it will work in human-rights cases.”
“The strategy beat the market in a bull run, so it will beat the market in a recession.”

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Ask what the argument takes for granted
Spot it: “just as…”, “similarly”, or an inference from one case/group to a different one
Match to answer language: “fails to consider relevant differences between the things compared”
Reject answers that attack premises
correctLooksLike: “fails to consider relevant differences between the things compared”
traps: Answers naming a different flaw that “sounds” similar
Answers that dispute a premise
commonError: Accepting an analogy because of surface similarities.

card.front: [Icon: scales with a circle and a square] Name this flaw.
